cards.front: What may you do at a pedestrian-activated crosswalk signal when all its lights are dark?
cards.back: At a pedestrian-activated crosswalk signal with all lights dark, you may proceed with caution if the crosswalk is clear.

cards.front: Why can a pedestrian often see a car before its driver sees the pedestrian?
cards.back: When you are the pedestrian, you can often see an approaching vehicle more easily than its driver can see you, especially at night, at dusk and dawn, and in bad weather.

cards.front: What should a pedestrian never assume about an approaching vehicle?
cards.back: As a pedestrian, never assume an approaching vehicle has seen you and will yield.

cards.front: Where should pedestrians cross?
cards.back: Pedestrians should use crosswalks where they exist or cross at an intersection.

cards.front: What should a pedestrian try to do with approaching drivers?
cards.back: Whenever possible, a pedestrian should make eye contact with the drivers of approaching vehicles.

cards.front: Why should a pedestrian look before stepping into the road, even at a crosswalk?
cards.back: Look before stepping into the road, because even at a crosswalk drivers need time to notice you and react.

cards.front: Which distractions should pedestrians avoid while crossing?
cards.back: Pedestrians should avoid distractions such as phones, headphones or earbuds while crossing.

cards.front: Where should a pedestrian cross at night, and what rules apply?
cards.back: At night, cross in a well-lit spot, and always follow the traffic rules, signs and signals where you cross.

cards.front: Where must you stop when driving out of an alley or driveway?
cards.back: When you drive out of an alley or driveway onto the road, you must stop before reaching the sidewalk.

cards.front: After stopping at the sidewalk, whom must you yield to before entering the road?
cards.back: After stopping at the sidewalk, yield to pedestrians and to approaching vehicles before entering the road.

cards.front: How does yielding when leaving a driveway differ from yielding on a left turn?
cards.back: Leaving an alley or driveway you stop before the sidewalk and then yield, while turning left you yield to oncoming vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians.
cards.memory_hook: stop then yield; yield on left

cards.front: Whom must you yield to when turning left?
cards.back: When turning left, you must yield to any oncoming vehicle, bicycle or pedestrian.

cards.front: When is a U-turn allowed?
cards.back: A U-turn is allowed when you can make it safely, it will not get in the way of other traffic, and no sign forbids it.

cards.front: What three things make a U-turn illegal?
cards.back: A U-turn is legal unless a sign bans it, it cannot be made safely, or it would interfere with other traffic.

cards.front: What must you do while making a U-turn?
cards.back: When making a U-turn, yield to approaching traffic and turn only when it is safe.

cards.front: What program might a red-light citation make you eligible for?
cards.back: A citation for running a red light or another civil traffic violation may make you eligible for the Arizona Supreme Court's Defensive Driving Program, so read the papers that come with the citation.

cards.front: Where do you learn about the Defensive Driving Program option after a citation?
cards.back: A red-light or other civil traffic citation may make you eligible for the Defensive Driving Program, and the options are explained in the papers that come with the citation.

cards.front: What must you attend after a conviction for running a red or flashing red light?
cards.back: A conviction for running a red light or a flashing red light means you must attend Traffic Survival School.

cards.front: What happens after you finish Traffic Survival School successfully?
cards.back: MVD is told when you finish Traffic Survival School successfully, and no further court appearance is then required.

cards.front: What must MVD order for every red-light conviction a court reports?
cards.back: By law, MVD must order Traffic Survival School for every red-light conviction the courts report.

cards.front: Who orders Traffic Survival School after a red-light conviction, and what if you skip it?
cards.back: Traffic Survival School is ordered by MVD after a red-light conviction, and skipping it ends in an indefinite suspension.

cards.front: What else does a red-light conviction add to your driver record?
cards.back: A red-light conviction also adds points, which appear on your driver record.

cards.front: What does paying a red-light fine mean?
cards.back: Paying the fine means accepting responsibility for the violation, and it is reported to MVD as a conviction.

cards.front: Is paying a red-light fine a quiet way out?
cards.back: Paying a red-light fine is not a quiet way out: it is reported to MVD as a conviction and points go on the record.

cards.front: What happens if you do not complete Traffic Survival School?
cards.back: Not completing Traffic Survival School leads to an indefinite suspension of your driving privilege.

cards.front: How do the penalties differ for a red-light crash with life-threatening injuries and one that causes death?
cards.back: A red-light crash with life-threatening injuries carries up to five hundred dollars and three months of suspension, while a crash causing death carries up to one thousand dollars and six months.

cards.front: What penalties may follow a crash you cause in which someone dies?
cards.back: If you cause a crash in which another driver or passenger dies, you may be fined up to one thousand dollars, have your driving privilege suspended for six months and be ordered to do community service.

cards.front: Where should you be especially alert for emergency vehicles?
cards.back: Stay alert for emergency vehicles, especially at intersections.

cards.front: What should you do when an emergency vehicle approaches with a siren or lights?
cards.back: When a police car, fire engine, ambulance or other emergency vehicle approaches with a siren, lights or other warning device, yield, move to the right side of the road and stop until it has passed.

cards.front: On a four-lane highway, how do you yield to an emergency vehicle in your direction?
cards.back: On a four-lane highway with at least two lanes going the same way as the emergency vehicle, proceed with due caution and yield by moving into a lane that is not next to its lane.

cards.front: What if you cannot safely change lanes for an emergency vehicle on a four-lane highway?
cards.back: If that lane change is impossible or unsafe, proceed with due caution and reduce your speed.

cards.front: How does yielding to an emergency vehicle differ on an ordinary road and a four-lane highway?
cards.back: With an approaching emergency vehicle on an ordinary road you pull right and stop, while on a four-lane highway with two lanes in its direction you move to a lane not next to it.

cards.front: How far behind a responding fire department vehicle must you stay?
cards.back: Keep at least five hundred feet behind a fire department vehicle that is responding to an emergency.

cards.front: How far behind a responding police vehicle must you stay?
cards.back: Keep at least three hundred feet behind a police vehicle that is responding to an emergency.

cards.front: How do the following distances differ behind fire and police emergency vehicles?
cards.back: The following distance behind an emergency fire department vehicle is five hundred feet, while behind an emergency police vehicle it is three hundred feet.

cards.front: Where may you not drive or park when an emergency vehicle has stopped to respond?
cards.back: Do not drive into or park in the block where an emergency vehicle has stopped to respond to an emergency.

cards.front: What does the move-over law require when you pass a vehicle stopped with flashing lights?
cards.back: The move-over law requires you to shift over one lane to leave a safe margin when you pass any vehicle with flashing lights stopped at the side of a road or highway.

cards.front: What must you do if moving over is unsafe or impossible?
cards.back: If moving over is unsafe or impossible, you must slow down and use caution instead.

cards.front: Under the move-over law, when do you slow down instead of changing lanes?
cards.back: Under the move-over law you change one lane away, and only if that is unsafe or impossible do you slow down and use caution instead.

cards.front: Which vehicles does the move-over law cover?
cards.back: The move-over law covers every pulled-over vehicle with flashing lights, including emergency-response and police vehicles, tow trucks, highway maintenance vehicles and private vehicles.

cards.front: What kind of vehicle does the move-over law apply to?
cards.back: The move-over law is about driving past a vehicle that is already pulled over at the roadside with its flashing lights on, whatever kind of vehicle it is.

cards.front: On which roads does the move-over law apply?
cards.back: The move-over law applies on all freeways and other multi-lane highways and on city roads and streets.

cards.front: Which funeral processions must you yield to?
cards.back: You must yield to any vehicle in a funeral procession led by a funeral escort vehicle flashing a red or blue light.

cards.front: When must you stop for a school bus picking up or dropping off passengers?
cards.back: When you approach a school bus that is picking up or dropping off passengers, stop completely before reaching it, whichever direction you are traveling.

cards.front: How does a loading school bus signal that it is stopped?
cards.back: A school bus loading or unloading passengers shows alternating flashing lights and an extended mechanical stop-sign arm.

cards.front: How long must you stay stopped for a school bus?
cards.back: Stay stopped until the school bus moves on or until its stop-sign arm and flashing lights are withdrawn.

cards.front: What two signals release you from a stopped school bus?
cards.back: A stopped school bus is released when it moves on or when both its stop-sign arm and flashing lights are put away.

cards.front: Why must you watch both ends of a stopped school bus?
cards.back: Watch for children crossing in front of or behind a stopped school bus, since a child may dart out from either end.

cards.front: When do you not have to stop for a school bus?
cards.back: On a divided roadway you do not have to stop for a school bus when you are traveling in the opposite direction.

cards.front: What makes a roadway divided for the school bus rule?
cards.back: A divided roadway is separated by a physical barrier such as a fence, curbing or a gap in the pavement; painted striping alone does not count.

cards.front: Do painted lines make a roadway divided for the school bus rule?
cards.back: Oncoming drivers may pass a loading school bus only on a roadway divided by a physical barrier; painted lines alone leave everyone required to stop.

cards.front: On a divided roadway, which school buses may you pass with caution?
cards.back: On a divided roadway you may proceed with caution past a school bus in the approaching lanes, but not past one stopped on your side of traffic.

cards.front: What must you do about speed regulations?
cards.back: Every speed regulation must be obeyed, and you should be prepared to change your speed quickly when needed.

recap_hooks.text: As a pedestrian, never assume a driver sees you; make eye contact, look first and skip the distractions.
Stop before the sidewalk leaving a driveway, yield on left turns, and make a U-turn only when it is safe, clear and allowed.
A red-light conviction means Traffic Survival School and points, paying the fine counts as a conviction, and skipping the school means indefinite suspension.
Pull right and stop for an emergency vehicle, and stay five hundred feet behind fire vehicles and three hundred behind police vehicles.
Move over a lane for any vehicle stopped with flashing lights, or slow down if you cannot, and yield to funeral processions.
Stop for a loading school bus until it moves or retracts its arm and lights, unless you are going the other way on a physically divided road.
